title: Mad libs
description: Our junior developer wrote MAD LIBS 3000, a cutting-edge storytelling engine in C. You give it a name, a colour and an object, and it spins you an epic tale of heroism, breakfast and a deeply disappointed cat. It works fine for most people... until someone curious or naughty steps in. Now, it's your job to be that curious—and perhaps naughty—person, and find out how to make this program break and behave in ways the developer never intended.
As you try and complete this challenge, you can understand the various ways in which this program can cause critical problems which we don't want!
hints: Look closely at the three scanf calls. Is one of them not like the others?
Each box only has room for 20 characters. What happens if your object is a LOT longer than that? Try watching what happens to the colour and the name in the story as your object gets longer.
Keep going. Somewhere past around 100 characters, the program stops telling stories altogether.
writeup: The name and colour are read with scanf("%19s", ...), which tells C to read at most 19 characters (leaving 1 spot for the \0 that marks the end of a string). But the object is read with a plain scanf("%s", object), which has no limit at all. It will happily keep writing whatever you type into memory, even long after the 20-byte object box is full. This is called a buffer overflow.

The three arrays live next to each other on the stack, a region of memory where a function keeps its local variables. When your object is too long, the extra characters spill over into whatever sits next to it. If you try an object of 40, 60 or 80 A's, you'll see the story start to change: first the hero's body turns AAAAAAAA instead of your colour, and then the hero's name itself becomes AAAAAAAA. You never typed those as the name or colour, but the object overwrote them! In a real program, this is how an attacker could change a variable like is_admin or a password without ever being asked for it.

Keep going and the overflow reaches something much more important. Also stored on the stack is the return address, which tells the CPU where to jump back to once main finishes. With roughly 104+ characters, your A's overwrite it with 0x4141414141414141 (0x41 is the letter A). When main returns, the CPU tries to jump to that nonsense address, the operating system steps in and kills the program with a segmentation fault. A careful attacker wouldn't use A's, though. They would carefully choose the bytes so the program jumps to code of their choosing, which is how many real-world exploits take over a machine.

The fix is simple: give every scanf a width limit, so scanf("%19s", object) instead of scanf("%s", object). It's also good practice to check that scanf actually returned 1 (meaning it read something). For reading whole lines, fgets(object, sizeof(object), stdin) is another safe option, because it always respects the size of the buffer.
